sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: GraphQL is increasingly chosen for client-facing APIs where consumers have varying data requirements — mobile apps, BFF layers, and internal developer tools. gqlgen is the dominant schema-first GraphQL server for Go, generating type-safe resolver interfaces from .graphql schema files. Interviewers probe this module to test whether you understand the N+1 query problem that is endemic to naive GraphQL resolvers, how dataloaders batch and cache those queries, and how subscriptions enable real-time updates. Knowing when to choose GraphQL over REST, and its operational tradeoffs (query complexity, introspection risks, caching difficulty), positions you as someone who has thought seriously about API design rather than just followed a tutorial.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body: gqlgen reads your .graphql schema and generates a models_gen.go with Go structs and a generated.go with resolver interfaces. You implement only the non-trivial resolvers by filling in resolver.go. The execution engine resolves each field by calling its resolver function; for object fields like user.posts, if each user triggers a separate SELECT for posts, you get N+1 queries. DataLoader (graph-gophers/dataloader or vikstrous/dataloadgen) solves this by accumulating all the user IDs requested in a single request tick, then batching them into one SELECT WHERE id IN (...) and distributing results back. Subscriptions use a WebSocket transport; the resolver returns a <-chan Event channel that the execution engine reads from and streams to the client.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body: 1. Schema-first vs code-first — gqlgen is schema-first: .graphql is the source of truth, Go code is generated. 2. Resolver interface — gqlgen generates a Resolver interface; you implement it; the framework wires it to the HTTP handler via NewExecutableSchema. 3. N+1 problem — loading a list of N objects each triggers a child resolver; without batching = N+1 database queries. 4. DataLoader pattern — per-request loader accumulates keys during resolver execution, flushes as a batch after a tick, caches within the request. 5. gqlgen middleware — field middleware via extension.FieldInterceptor; request middleware via transport or handler wrappers. 6. Subscriptions — define subscription in schema; resolver returns <-chan *model.Event; client connects via WebSocket (graphql-ws protocol). 7. Query complexity limiting — gqlgen's complexity extension assigns a cost per field; requests exceeding the limit are rejected before execution. 8. Introspection in production — disable or restrict to avoid leaking schema to attackers; gqlgen supports handler.Option to disable it.

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body: Q: What is the N+1 problem in GraphQL and how do you fix it? — Each object in a list triggers a child resolver; 100 users triggers 100 queries for their posts. Fix with a DataLoader that batches all requested IDs into a single query per request. Q: How does gqlgen's schema-first approach differ from code-first libraries? — The .graphql schema is committed as the contract; code is derived from it. Code-first derives the schema from Go types, which can lead to unintended schema changes when Go structs change. Q: How would you implement authentication in a gqlgen server? — Use an HTTP middleware to parse and validate the JWT, inject the user into the request context; read it from context inside resolvers using a typed context key. Q: Why is HTTP caching difficult with GraphQL? — All queries go to the same POST /graphql endpoint, making URL-based CDN caching impossible; persisted queries with GET + query hash can restore some caching. Q: When would you choose REST over GraphQL? — Public APIs where clients are external and should not control query shape, cacheable resources, or when the team is more familiar with REST tooling and HTTP semantics.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: "I use gqlgen because it's schema-first — the .graphql file is the contract that frontend and backend teams agree on before writing any Go code, and it generates type-safe resolver stubs so there's no chance of a mismatch between schema and implementation. The first thing I do after getting a basic server working is wire up DataLoaders for every resolver that fetches a child entity — the N+1 problem will show up in production the moment you have more than a handful of records. I scope each DataLoader to the request context so it doesn't cache across requests. For subscriptions I use the graphql-ws WebSocket protocol with a channel-based resolver; the resolver goroutine sends events to the channel and closes it when the subscription ends. I also always enable the complexity extension with a sensible limit — without it a single deeply nested query can lock up the server."
